title: Sabyasachi Hosts First Diwali Reception at Met Museum in New York
excerpt: Rani Mukerji and Masaba Gupta joined the October 21 celebration, the first Diwali event at the Met and the latest chapter in Sabyasachi's multi-year collaboration with the museum.
body:
• Designer Sabyasachi hosted a Diwali reception at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York on October 21, the first Diwali event held at the museum.
  • Rani Mukerji and Masaba Gupta were among the guests reported at the celebration, according to India Today and the Free Press Journal.
  • The reception follows Sabyasachi's multi-year collaboration with the Met, including a fine jewellery collection unveiled at New York Fashion Week.
  • For diaspora readers in New York, Diwali is on Sunday, November 8 this year, with the five-day festival beginning with Dhanteras.

Designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee hosted a Diwali reception at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York on October 21, marking the first time a Diwali event has been held at the museum, according to reporting on luxury brands and Diwali. India Today reported Rani Mukerji and Masaba Gupta among the guests bringing what it described as desi glamour to the evening in New York.

The setting matters. The Met is one of the United States' defining cultural institutions, and a Diwali reception there places the festival alongside the other cultural moments the museum marks publicly. For Indian Americans in the New York area, it is a visible signal that Diwali is no longer confined to temples, community halls and home celebrations.

A collaboration years in the making

Sabyasachi has been working with the Met for several years. That relationship became public in a new form at New York Fashion Week, when the designer returned after 18 years and unveiled the first chapter of a multi-year collaboration translating works from the museum's collection into contemporary high jewellery through Indian goldsmithing and gem-setting techniques.

Coverage of that show described monumental pieces including the Pantokrator Pendant, inspired by an 11th- to 12th-century Byzantine ivory carving, and a Zodiac Rivière inspired by Mughal emperor Jahangir's zodiac coinage. Rani Mukerji attended that show from the front row in a black saree. The Diwali reception extends the same partnership from the runway into the museum itself.

"India shops by occasion, not by season. Diwali is the biggest occasion of all: the one moment when buying something new is auspicious rather than indulgent, and when much of what you buy, you give away."

— Sumeet Yadav, Reliance Brands Limited

Diwali moves onto luxury's global calendar

The Met reception was one of several New York Diwali fixtures this season. Cartier again hosted an annual Diwali event at its Fifth Avenue Mansion, Anjula Acharia's All That Glitters ball returned, and Oushq marked the festival on October 19 with an evening co-hosted by Pritika Swarup and the Council of Fashion Designers of America at The Standard Hotel.

Analysts quoted in the Vogue Business reporting on Diwali and luxury put India's luxury market at around $12 billion, according to Euromonitor International, and ranked India among the world's five fastest-growing luxury markets. That commercial weight, combined with one of the world's largest diasporas, explains why brands that have long built campaigns around Ramadan and Lunar New Year are now learning Diwali.

The same reporting sounded a caution. Jessel Taank, publicist for Oushq, said New York's celebrations are still driven more by individuals than by brands, and advised international houses to work with someone who understands the festival and can lead the narrative. The Sabyasachi reception was cited as an example of that approach: a designer who knows the festival working directly with a cultural institution.

What it means for the diaspora

For readers celebrating in the United States, the practical calendar is unchanged: Diwali's main day, Lakshmi Puja, falls on Sunday, November 8 this year, and the five-day festival begins with Dhanteras, an auspicious occasion for buying gold and jewellery, before culminating in Bhai Dooj. What the Met event changes is visibility. When a festival is hosted inside a national museum, school holidays, workplace leave and public celebrations become easier conversations for families who have long had to explain them.

London offered a contrast this season, with a quieter luxury calendar despite regular fixtures such as the UK-India Creative Circle party at the Royal Automobile Club on October 30. Dubai, home to a large wealthy Indian community, was also described as muted. New York, this year, carried the moment — and Sabyasachi, at the Met, carried New York.
